title: Process for exporting cell-cultivated products of animal origin from Great Britain to non-EU countries
text:
Summary 

 Cell-cultivated products made from animal cells are considered to be Products of Animal Origin ( POAO ) for regulatory purposes, consistent with Food Standards Agency and Food Standards Scotland guidance on classification and Hazard Analysis Critical Control Points ( HACCP ) principles , although this classification is not explicitly specified in legislation.

 This guidance explains the steps you should take to export cell-cultivated POAO from Great Britain ( GB ) to non-EU countries. It signposts further information to help you through the process. 

 We recommend that you also read the full step-by-step guide on exports from UK .

 This guidance describes the process for exporting cell-cultivated products derived from animal cells from Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales). References to the UK are used where relevant requirements apply across all UK nations.

 As different regulatory requirements may apply in Northern Ireland under the Windsor Framework, if you are a business intending to export cell-cultivated products from Northern Ireland you should seek advice on the requirements that apply to your circumstances. 

 Cell-cultivated products do not currently benefit from internationally recognised sanitary and phytosanitary classifications or established export certification arrangements. Consequently, unlike many traditional animal-derived products, there are no standard export certificate templates specifically for cell-cultivated products.

 While this process map draws on the requirements that typically apply to POAO , cell-cultivated product export applications are likely to be assessed on a case-by-case basis and may require engagement with destination country’s competent authorities to determine the applicable import, certification and market access requirements.

 The process map relates to cell-cultivated products exported from GB for placement on the market in non-EU jurisdictions. Depending on the destination country’s regulatory framework, placement on the market may require a novel food authorisation or another form of pre-market approval.

 Regulatory classification 

 Cell-cultivated products are not defined as ‘meat’. For regulatory purposes, the Food Standards Agency and Food Standards Scotland considers cell-cultivated products derived from animal cells to fall within the scope of POAO , although Regulation (EC) 853/2004 does not explicitly classify them as such.

 The Food Standards Agency and Food Standards Scotland published this position in December 2025, in cell-cultivated products: guidance on classification and HACCP principles . It applies to products regulated in GB . Countries you export to may apply different classifications for their own import controls and market access. 

 When you harvest cell-cultivated biomass (cells harvested from the bioreactor), you process it. This means cell-cultivated products count as processed POAO or composite products. The Food Standards Agency and Food Standards Scotland published this position in July 2026, in cell-cultivated products: food business hygiene requirements .

 Legislation 

 The main UK regulations that apply are: 

 • Regulation (EU) 2015/2283 - Novel Foods

 • Regulation (EC) 853/2004 - Hygiene of Foodstuffs of Animal Origin

 • Regulation (EC) 852/2004 - General Hygiene of Foodstuffs

 • Regulation (EC) 178/2002 - General Food Law

 • Regulation (EU) 2017/625 - Official Controls

 • Trade in Animals and Related Products (“TARP”) Regulations 2011 (SI No.1197/2011)

 • Trade in Animals and Related Products (Scotland) Regulations 2012 (SSI 2012 No.177)

 • Trade in Animals and Related Products (Wales) Regulations 2011 (SI No. 2011/2379)

 Process map: exporting cell-cultivated POAO from Great Britain to non-EU countries  

 This process map outlines the steps you should take to export cell-cultivated products produced in Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales) to other countries.

 Different requirements may apply if you’re exporting from Northern Ireland under the Windsor Framework, and different requirements apply depending on whether you’re exporting to EU, Northern Ireland or non-EU countries.  

 Import requirements for cell-cultivated products are evolving internationally and vary between countries. You should always check current requirements with the competent authority in your destination country before you export. 

 This document is intended to provide an indicative overview of potential export requirements and processes. It is not a substitute for the relevant legislation, official guidance issued by competent authorities, or independent legal advice. In the event of any inconsistency between this document and applicable legislation or destination-country requirements, the legislation and destination-country requirements shall take precedence.

 Export pathways for these products are still being developed and tested, so some steps may change as we gain experience and export systems become established. Following this process does not guarantee that you’ll be able to export, that certification will be available, or that your destination country will approve the import of your product.

 Export requirements depend on the laws and import conditions of your destination country, and on decisions made by the relevant competent authorities.

 As the export pathways for cell-cultivated products are being tested, feedback from industry on this guidance will help us to refine and update it where necessary. Contact exported.food@food.gov.uk if you have information that would be useful to add to the process map.

 Step 1: check destination country eligibility and market access

 You and the importer at your destination country must work together to check whether you can import cell-cultivated products into that country. 

 Confirm that your destination country accepts cell-cultivated products. Compliance with UK law does not create a right to export. In GB , we classify cell-cultivated products as POAO , which aligns to current EU classification. Other countries may classify cell-cultivated products differently.  

 When you’re checking this, consider: 

 • whether cell-cultivated products are permitted for import and sale 

 • how your destination country classifies cell-cultivated products for import purposes 

 • whether the destination country has published official import conditions 

 • whether market access arrangements exist 

 See exporting country guides . 

 You can also submit an export query online .

 Market access must be established for exports to take place. Businesses may initiate requests for market access, while formal negotiations on import requirements are generally conducted between the competent authorities of the exporting and importing countries.

 Where market access for cell-cultivated products has not yet been established, contact the relevant team at the Animal and Plant Health Agency ( APHA ) Centre for International Trade . They can advise you on whether you need government-to-government engagement to clarify import conditions.

 Related guidance

 Get help with your export query .

 Step 2: confirm GB establishment eligibility

 You must make sure that your GB -based production establishment complies with applicable GB food law requirements, as well as any requirements imposed by the destination country. In GB , cell-cultivated product production establishments must be registered with the relevant local authority as food businesses. 

 Destination countries may also require your establishment to be registered, listed or approved for export to their market. These requirements are separate from GB food business registration and vary between jurisdictions.

 You should: 

 • register your food business with the relevant local authority

 • confirm whether any activities carried out at your establishment are subject to additional approval or authorisation requirements 

 • check whether your production establishment meets the destination country’s export requirements 

 • verify those requirements directly with the destination country’s competent authority  

 Related guidance and legislation

 Cell-cultivated products: food business hygiene requirements .

 Regulation (EC) 178/2002, Articles 12 (Food and feed exported from the Community), 17 (Food business operator responsibilities).

 Step 3: confirm product eligibility and SPS requirements

 Check that your cell-cultivated product meets the destination country’s import, marketing, SPS and certification requirements. 

 Your consignment may be subject to official controls undertaken by the competent authority under Regulation (EU) 2017/625 if these controls are applicable to the product and establishment concerned.

 In addition, the consignment must comply with any of the requirements of the destination country, which may impose different or additional inspection or documentary requirements. 

 Check product authorisation requirements 

 You should contact the destination country’s competent authority to confirm: 

 • what type of food marketing authorisation, novel food approval, GMO approval (if applicable), taste-trial approval or equivalent you need

 • whether your product falls within any commodity-specific import controls the destination country applies 

 Check product compliance requirements 

 You should: 

 • find out the destination country’s SPS requirements, as officials will check these at origin or point of dispatch, including your declaration status and any risk flags 

 • follow any traceability and record-keeping requirements set by the destination country, your product authorisation, import permit or certification requirements 

 • check for any restrictions or safeguard measures affecting your commodity 

 Check labelling and market requirements 

 You should check: 

 • the destination country’s labelling requirements 

 • any cell-cultivated product-specific labelling requirements that apply 

 Prepare supporting evidence 

 You should: 

 • have evidence ready for any official assurances, attestations or certification requirements the destination country specifies 

 • make sure your product meets GB food safety and hygiene legislation, where the importing country requires this 

 Related legislation

 • Regulation (EU) 2017/625, Article 1.3 (Subject matter and scope)

 • Regulation (EC) 178/2002, Articles 12 (Food and feed exported from the Community), 17-19 (Food business operator responsibilities)

 Step 4: export health certification (if required by destination country)

 Find out whether the destination country requires an Export Health Certificate ( EHC ), other official certification, or if it does not require any government-issued certification.

 If you need official certification, get the relevant certificate before you export. We issue EHCs under UK export certification arrangements. The specific requirements we certify relate to products made in GB , and these requirements can differ depending on the destination country. 

 Find out what certification you need 

 If the destination country requires official certification, contact the importing country’s central authority to find out their certification requirements. 

 If you need an EHC , you should: 

 • get the specific EHC requirements from the importing country’s central authority 

 • check whether they match any existing certification 

 • if not, ask APHA to draft a new certification (see ‘If an EHC does not yet exist for your product and destination country’ below) 

 If you’re moving products within GB before export 

 You may need supporting health attestations to get the necessary assurances if you move products from your production premises before dispatch. 

 If an EHC does not yet exist for your product and destination country 

 Contact APHA using the get help with animal and plant health service to provide the import requirements and request a new EHC .
